news.title: Oprah washes her hands of protégé Dr Phil
news.text:
“People criticise me for Dr. Phil and Dr. Oz, because of their politics or their views,” the billionaire media mogul told Emmy magazine in an interview published last Tuesday.

“Everybody has their own path in life, and it has not one thing to do with me, and I don’t have one thing to do with them.”

The distancing is striking because Winfrey was instrumental in introducing both men to a mass audience on The Oprah Winfrey Show before her Harpo Productions helped turn them into stand-alone television brands.

Winfrey acknowledged as much, saying the reason she gave both men their “breaks” was that she believed they had information worth sharing.

“At the time, the reason and intention behind me giving them their breaks was I thought they had valuable information to share that had been meaningful to me,” Winfrey said.

McGraw’s relationship with Winfrey dates to 1998, when he helped her during a six-week Texas trial stemming from a lawsuit filed by cattlemen who accused her of defaming the beef industry.

“Dr Phil, he was so practical, so down to earth, so real,” Winfrey told Emmy.

“And he would ride in the car with me every morning on the way to trial, where I’m literally sitting on trial for six weeks.”

Winfrey said McGraw’s advice made such an impression that she decided to put him before her viewers.

“I felt that he was so instrumental in helping me,” she said. “I thought, ‘Oh, you could help a lot of people. You should come on my show.’”

McGraw became one of Oprah’s most familiar experts, ultimately logging 118 appearances, according to official statistics from the show.

His first book, “Life Strategies,” became a bestseller in 1999, with Publishers Weekly crediting Oprah’s endorsement as one factor behind its success.

Harpo then created Dr. Phil, which premiered in September 2002 as the first spin-off from The Oprah Winfrey Show.

The show became a daytime juggernaut, ranking behind only Oprah for nine seasons before taking over as the syndicated daytime-talk leader after Winfrey ended her show in 2011.

But McGraw’s public profile has taken a pronounced political turn in recent years.

He appeared at Trump’s Madison Square Garden campaign rally in October 2024, where he defended Trump and his supporters, although he later insisted the appearance was not an endorsement and declined to reveal how he voted.

McGraw subsequently accompanied Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel during an enforcement operation in Chicago alongside Trump border czar Tom Homan.

Trump appointed McGraw to his Religious Liberty Commission in May of last year.

Winfrey, by contrast, has repeatedly backed Democrats even while describing herself as a registered independent. She endorsed Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris and campaigned for Stacey Abrams in Georgia.

The political split with Oz is even more explicit.

Winfrey said longtime pal Gayle King first introduced her to the heart surgeon, whose skill at translating medical subjects for ordinary viewers convinced her to bring him onto the show.

“Gayle introduced me to Dr. Oz,” Winfrey told Emmy. “He explained practical things like colon cancer and bowel movements.”

“I thought he had the language for explaining medical things in a way that was helpful to me. I thought it would be helpful to many other people.”

Oz began appearing on Oprah in 2004 and became one of the program’s most recognisable medical experts.

Harpo later produced The Dr. Oz Show with Sony, helping transform him from a recurring TV doctor into a nationally syndicated star.

Harpo and Oz also became co-founders of the digital-health company Sharecare alongside Sony, Discovery and other partners.

Oz eventually entered Republican politics, running for US Senate in Pennsylvania in 2022 as a conservative Republican after earlier describing himself as more moderate.

Trump endorsed Oz in the GOP primary, which he won before losing the general election to Democrat John Fetterman.

Winfrey made clear where she stood in that race.

Just days before the election, she publicly endorsed Fetterman over the man whose television career she had helped propel.

Oz later returned to Washington as an appointee of the Trump administration.

The Senate confirmed him in April 2025 as administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, giving the former Oprah regular direct authority over one of the federal government’s biggest health agencies.

The Post has sought comment from Winfrey, Oz and McGraw.

news.title: Fast Takes- The unmaking of Jason Arday, the left declares war on parents and other commentary
news.text:
Campus watch: The Unmaking of Jason Arday

Though he “cannot help but feel bad for [Jason] Arday and his family,” American Greatness’ Roger Kimball also can’t “forget that his fabulations were directed not only at aggrandizing himself”: The professor was “perfectly happy to play the race card to damage others, as when he complained to the police that journalists who were investigating his credentials were guilty of harassing him,” prompting “a four-month-long investigation into a journalist who was simply going about his job.” Claims his apparent suicide creates “a debate about whether he was a plagiarist or victim of a racial witch hunt” present “a false dichotomy. There is no doubt that Arday was a plagiarist,” and he was a victim only “of his own lies and intemperate behavior” — as well as of “an educational establishment” that “colluded in the construction of Arday’s fantastical, self-aggrandizing and ultimately self-destructive fantasies.”

Education beat: The Left Declares War on Parents

“I almost didn’t believe what I heard. Samuel Moyn, a professor at Yale Law School, told an interviewer that parents can’t be trusted because they have a ‘divergence of interest’ with their own children,” marvels Lincoln Fillmore at The Wall Street Journal. Legally, “parents bear the primary responsibility for educating children.” When they enroll “a child in school,” parents “aren’t transferring responsibility,” they are “choosing a partner to help fulfill it.” Unlike educators, parents have “a lifelong commitment” to their child. So “the strongest schools understand they are joining families in a shared mission” and that “the parents are in charge.” Bottom line: No person “will ever match a parent’s depth of understanding, love or willingness to sacrifice when navigating the inevitable ‘diverging interests’ between parent and child.”

Eye on ’28: This May Be AOC’s Best Chance

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is now the left’s “best-known and most popular national figure,” observes The Washington Post’s Henry Olsen, and progressives’ “impressive string of primary victories” this year raises her odds in a 2028 presidential run. Other potential Democratic candidates — Kamala Harris, Pete Buttigieg, Gavin Newsom — can “tack leftward,” but none can “compete with AOC’s authentic devotion to her causes.” Yet even a damaged 2028 GOP may see her nomination as “a dream come true” — and AOC shouldn’t run if she’s “ambivalent”: Running for and serving as US president requires “an all-consuming ambition.” But if she really “harbors the dream,” she’d best “seize a moment that may never come again and jump in.”

Conservative: A Fake Israel Supporter

“Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro’s Jewishness” could “hold him back from being embraced as a national figure in the Democratic Party” — and a 2028 prez primary could see him “passed over after the party’s progressive base launched attacks on his Jewishness,” notes Commentary’s Seth Mandel. Now that Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff is “surrounded” by “presidential chatter,” he too must expect “scrutiny” of his “position on Israel.” As the Hamas war progressed, “Ossoff’s voting record started to split”; he even took to retailing the “revolting libel” that Gaza was being “starved” by Israel, with no apology yet. Ossoff “demeans himself and insults the Jewish community when he goes around saying he supports the Jewish state.”

Psychotherapist: Autism Is Not an Identity

The widespread “assumption that psychiatric diagnoses, especially those for ADHD and autism, can and do pick out objective conditions that psychiatrists accurately diagnose,” is, “aside from a small number of diagnoses,” just “not the case,” explains James Barnes at Spiked. That is: “No clinician examining an individual could identify and distinguish an ‘ADHD brain’ from a ‘normal brain,’” and “no neuroscientist can look at an individual’s brain scan and determine that a person is autistic.” This is a “diagnosis describing a person’s behavior”; treating it as “an identity” is “based on the misunderstanding that it is explanatory” even “for personality, relationships and sometimes almost every aspect of a person’s life.”

— Compiled by The Post Editorial Board

news.title: How Gavin Newsom loses every primary state in 2028
news.text:
The Democratic National Committee this weekend reshuffled the opening rounds of its 2028 presidential primary — and Gavin Newsom probably shouldn’t be celebrating.

The new calendar sends Democratic presidential candidates through South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia before the race broadens on Super Tuesday in early March 2028.

For Newsom, that’s quite an itinerary. In state after state, opponents will have a chance to take pieces of the California record he has spent seven years championing and introduce them to Democratic voters who may be considerably less enthusiastic.

That matters because Newsom is no longer the bright, shiny object he was a year ago.

He mastered the art of trolling Donald Trump when Trump was riding high. He became a fixture on national television and even more dominant on social media, especially X, where sparring with the president became a daily political performance.

But lately, national Democrats don’t seem nearly as excited about what Newsom is selling.

A July Emerson poll put Pete Buttigieg first at 19%, Newsom second at 17%, with Jon Ossoff and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at 13%. In New Hampshire, AOC led at 22%, one point ahead of Buttigieg.

Trump’s approval ratings have fallen, too. Attacking an unpopular Trump isn’t much of a specialty act anymore. Plenty of Democrats can do it.

If Newsom had any influence over the new calendar, it sure doesn’t show.

January 22 — South Carolina

Newsom starts where Democratic voters are less progressive on transgender issues than California.

A Winthrop University poll found 54% of South Carolina Democrats favored requiring transgender athletes to compete according to their sex at birth.

California still allows biological males who identify as female to compete in girls’ sports. When that produces an unfair result, Newsom embraced a workaround adding qualifying spots or medals for displaced female athletes.

He also signed legislation protecting access to sex-change procedures for minors, while taxpayer-funded Medi-Cal covers hormone therapy and sex-change surgeries.

February 1 — Nevada

Nevadans don’t have to wonder what Newsom’s energy policies might mean. Californian policy can hit them at the pump.

Nevada gets much of its fuel from California. In 2024, Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo and Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs warned Newsom that refinery rules could reduce supplies and raise gasoline prices in their states.

Welcome to Nevada, Governor. Let’s talk gas prices.

February 8 — New Hampshire

Next comes New Hampshire, where “Live Free or Die” still means something — including on energy.

Polling found 71% of New Hampshire Democrats favor an energy strategy combining renewables with natural gas.

California is heading the other way. Newsom’s regulators have pursued zero-emission standards for new furnaces and water heaters as part of a push to electrify buildings and move consumers away from natural gas.

Try selling forced electrification during a New Hampshire winter.

February 15 — New Mexico

Newsom directed California regulators to develop a plan to phase out oil extraction by 2045 and has repeatedly talked about moving California “beyond oil.”

New Mexico is America’s second-largest oil-producing state.

Democratic leaders there use the oil-and-gas bonanza to help finance education, healthcare, infrastructure and universal child care.

Newsom can explain why the industry helping pay for New Mexico Democrats’ agenda should eventually disappear.

February 22 — Michigan

Then Newsom reaches the auto capital.

He personally launched California’s effort to require all new passenger vehicles sold in the state to be zero-emission by 2035.

Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin thought California went too far. She was the only Senate Democrat to vote to overturn the mandate, citing more than one million Michiganders whose livelihoods depend on the auto industry.

Imagine Newsom explaining Sacramento’s vision of the car business in Detroit.

February 29 — Virginia

Finally comes Virginia, where Democratic voters are souring on subsidizing the massive data centers needed to power the AI boom.

A 2026 VCU poll found 73% of Virginia Democrats opposed maintaining the state’s sales-tax exemption for data centers.

Newsom has positioned California as the home of the AI revolution and vetoed a Democratic bill imposing new water-reporting requirements on data centers.

Then comes Super Tuesday on March 7, when the race broadens dramatically.

But Newsom first has to survive six states where parts of his California record could become liabilities.

Then, in January 2027, he loses the governorship — and the enormous platform that comes with it.

Meanwhile, Kamala Harris passed on running for governor, says she is considering another White House bid and continues building a national political presence.

Newsom faces a crowded field, a potential California rival and an opening calendar littered with pieces of his own record.

Newsom wanted California to be his calling card. It may become his baggage.

news.title: Most voters say they are worse off under Trump, new poll says
news.text:
Americans broadly believe that the economy is growing worse under President Donald Trump’s stewardship and say that they are personally worse off after a year and a half of his second presidency.

The findings are part of a poll conducted by Focaldata for the Financial Times and gauged Americans’ mood about Republican control of Washington as the midterms rapidly approach.

Overall, Americans of all political stripes say that they are in a financially worse position than they were on January 19, 2025, when Joe Biden concluded his presidency and prepared to hand over the keys. Roughly 53 percent of all registered voters, including nearly 25 percent of Republicans, said they were in a worse position now, as the war with Iran and other issues continue to drive up consumer costs, including the price of fuel.

The poll also found a clear advantage for Democrats on a midterm generic ballot, with 51 percent of Americans saying they’d vote for a Democrat over a Republican in November’s midterm elections. 45 percent preferred the Republican.

It’s a plethora of warning signs for Trump and his party as they seek to hold on to majorities in both chambers of Congress this fall. On the issue of jobs and the economy, more voters said they trusted Democrats over Republicans — possibly the worst sign in the poll for the GOP, which credited support on those issues for Trump’s victory over Kamala Harris in 2024.

The president’s approval rating remains grim. The poll found 55 percent of Americans disapprove of the job he’s doing, and his support among Republicans is slowly beginning to crack. 

One in five now disapprove of his performance so far through his second term. His approval rating among Republicans dropped eight points between this latest poll, released Sunday, and the Financial Times’ previous survey in July.

Democrats need to pick up four seats in the Senate and the same number in the House to win double majorities in Congress next year. Doing so in either chamber would effectively put a stop to any partisan legislation for the next two years, effectively neutering the GOP’s agenda apart from what the president and his Cabinet secretaries can achieve at the executive level.

The retaking of both chambers even theoretically opens the door to the possibility of a third round of impeachment proceedings, but Democratic leaders have backed away from such inclinations in public statements and interviews as the midterms approach.

More likely is the prospect of Democrats seeking to expose the administration to political damage through congressional investigations if they retake the House or Senate. Democrats have already pledged to investigate the Trump family’s financial dealings, which have included record-setting profits under his second presidency. 

Several committees are also eyeing congressional subpoena power to investigate the firings and institutional changes wrought by Elon Musk’s DOGE initiative.

Republicans have endured the narrowest margins in the House for more than a year, leaving the chamber constantly at war with itself and making passage of the “One Big, Beautiful Bill” last year an arduous task. The president, his team and the GOP’s united refusal to negotiate with Democrats on its policy objectives have also forced the party to achieve most of its policy gains through the budget reconciliation package, which is limited to budget-related issues but allows the 60-vote filibuster threshold to be avoided.

Trump has pushed Republicans to scrap the filibuster and hurriedly pass other legislation, to no avail.

This latest Financial Times survey comes on the heels of a Reuters/Ipsos survey that found support for the U.S. war with Iran to be extremely low, with a wide majority of Americans believing that Trump had failed to lay out his goals or his strategy.

The Financial Times poll was conducted between August 7 to August 10 with a survey pool of 1,913 registered voters. The margin of error was 2.9 percentage points.
news.summary: One in five Republicans say their finances are worse after year and a half of Trump
news.author: John Bowden

news.title: Woke 2.0 Will Be Worse
news.text:
Readers familiar with Dr. Seuss’s classic, The Cat in the Hat, will remember the twin chaos agents Thing 1 and Thing 2. “‘These Things are good Things,’” the Cat reassures the children whose mother has inexplicably left them under the supervision of a fish. “‘They are tame. Oh, so tame! / They have come here to play.’” The Things briefly feign innocence, then quickly reveal themselves to be marauding imps, knocking over nightstands and ruining the linens. “I do not like the way that they play!” says the son of the house.

Now here comes Woke 1 and Woke 2. “Woke 1 was crazy,” said U.S. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, quoting an unnamed city councilman in a viral interview for ABC. The congresswoman sheepishly acknowledged that Americans did not like the way Woke 1 played out, while also implicitly announcing that there will soon be, or already is, a Woke 2. And it will be tame. Oh, so tame!

There is, in fact, a new version of wokeness in the making. But just as Thing 2 was fundamentally identical to Thing 1, Woke 2 will not be any different in essence from Woke 1. They are both here to upend the furniture. Wokeness in all its forms is grievance politics. Its central idea is that an injustice lies at the heart of America and must be corrected to atone for the historical misery inflicted on groups of innocents.

What is changing in Woke 2 is the account of who those innocents are, and how they have been wronged. Woke 1 was founded on the notion that black women are the most oppressed, and therefore most righteous, of all people. “I’m thinking,” said Kamala Harris in her vice presidential victory speech, “about the generations of women—black women.” She mentioned many other kinds of women, of course, but the list began and ended with “the black women—who are too often overlooked, but so often prove that they are the backbone of this country.”
news.author: Beege Welborn

news.title: What Bezos did at the Washington Post could happen in NZ
news.text:
Pro-Trump media ownership is influencing journalism in the US. Think it couldn’t happen here? Anna Fifield argues developments over the past year say otherwise.

The walls inside the Washington Post building on K Street – the flash new premises provided by Jeff Bezos after he bought the newspaper in 2013 – are covered with inspirational quotes.

There’s this one, from Ben Bradlee, the editor-in-chief at the time of the Watergate scandal: “The truth, no matter how bad, is never as dangerous as a lie in the long run.”

And this: “There is only one good reason to enter journalism: When we do our job we can make a difference.” That’s from Don Graham, scion of the family that owned the Post for 80 years before selling it to Bezos.

Whenever I went back to head office during my years as Tokyo then Beijing bureau chief, and most recently as Asia editor, I found them inspiring. This was my calling. It might sound trite (or self important) but to this day, I believe that a free and flourishing press is crucial to democracy. 

On my last visit to the mothership, however, I noticed that a new inscription had appeared on the walls. It was from Bezos and it said: “What’s dangerous is not to evolve.”

At the time, I snickered, but I shrugged it off as an owner’s right to install himself among these lions of journalism.

After all, he’d been a great owner for the first 11 years: He had invested heavily in the Post and backed the Star Wars-sounding motto, Democracy Dies in Darkness, but had not inserted himself into editorial operations. It seemed he was truly interested in journalism as a democratic institution, rather than pursuing the Post as a vanity project (after all, he had his space programme for that).

I should have seen that quote on the wall as a portent. Boy, did he evolve in his ownership of the Post – and in ways that would soon feel dangerous.

In the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, Bezos would spike the Post’s endorsement of Kamala Harris, a decision that saw the exodus of several hundred thousand subscribers and many brand-name, Pulitzer Prize-winning journalists. 

Then came the Amazon founder’s edict that the Post’s opinion page would henceforth be devoted to “personal liberties and free markets”.

Another exodus. A round of devastating buyouts.

Then came the biggest blow of all: Some 375 journalists – including me – were laid off in a single day in February this year. It was brutal. Almost everyone on the international desk – including the entire China, Middle East, Ukraine teams – gone. Sports, gone. Books, gone. The flagship Post Reports podcast, gone. The local, climate, photo, technology and video desks were left as shells of their former selves. Almost half the newsroom disappeared overnight.

Cost cutting was the ostensible reason — although the Post is owned by one of the world’s richest men.

This same trend is occurring across the United States. Billionaire David Ellison bought the CBS network and appointed Bari Weiss, a right-wing columnist with no television experience, as editor-in-chief. It’s been haemorrhaging viewers, as well as journalists, who are complaining about pro-Trump editorial interference.

Ellison has now set his sights on Warner Bros. Discovery, the owner of CNN, a well-established global channel that Trump regularly labels a “corrupt organisation” that he says is publishing “fake news”.

That would make the overall media eco-system friendlier to Trump and his “alternative facts”. And that’s without even mentioning the pro-Trump propaganda over at Fox News, the president’s preferred TV channel, and the substantial reach he has with his all-caps, late-night blast medium, Truth Social.

It’s easy to look at what’s happening in the US as an aberration in their system, the result of an increasingly authoritarian president going unchecked by a cowed Congress. But we shouldn’t be too blasé. This past year has seen some worrying developments in New Zealand involving a seemingly politically-driven billionaire seeking media influence and a government that looked like it was attempting to intimidate media figures.

Canadian-born private equity billionaire Jim Grenon, a New Zealand resident who has backed anti-vax conspiracy theorists, is now the largest shareholder of NZME, owner of the New Zealand Herald and Newstalk ZB, and is a director on its board.

He may have failed in his board takeover attempt – at least for now – but he has continued to use his financial resources to fund challenges to other reporting he dislikes. 

He funded a defamation case taken by Julian Batchelor, the conspiracy theorist and organiser of the “Stop Co-Governance” roadshow, against TVNZ and disinformation expert Sanjana Hattotuwa – and tried to keep his involvement secret. In both cases, Grenon tried to shape NZ media and public discourse from behind the scenes, which is precisely what worried NZME’s board and shareholder groups from the outset.

Then there’s concerns about government attempts at interference.

Act leader and deputy prime minister David Seymour – who is also a shareholding minister for both RNZ and TVNZ – earlier this year sharply criticised the management of both state broadcasters.

Seymour attacked RNZ’s decision to appoint John Campbell as co-host of Morning Report, saying opinion pieces Campbell wrote while working for TVNZ should have put the idea of him hosting the flagship programme “out of the question”. Referring to RNZ chief executive Paul Thompson, Seymour said “that guy’s got an awful lot to answer for, and I suspect that he won’t be answering the call at RNZ for much longer”.

RNZ chairman Jim Mather strongly defended RNZ and its management, saying it is editorially independent, and indeed, legislation prohibits ministers from interfering in editorial decisions at RNZ or TVNZ. Seymour denies he stepped outside the bounds of law.

Fast forward, and Thompson has announced he’ll leave his position at the end of the year – a decision he said he made at the end of 2025, before Seymour weighed in – while Mather’s term came to an end last month.

Paul Goldsmith, the minister for media and communications, distanced himself from Seymour’s remarks, but has – at the same time – proposed changes that have also raised concerns about the erosion of standards and the institution of the media as a pillar of democracy. This includes closing the Broadcasting Standards Authority, the regulatory body governing radio and television – something experts have said is “politically expedient” and “democratically indefensible”.

None of these efforts have had any discernible effect on the way RNZ and TVNZ operate – and none of it is remotely comparable to the intimidation and interference happening in the US.

But if you had asked me three years ago if I could imagine Jeff Bezos prominently seated at Trump’s inauguration, then soon after aligning the Washington Post’s editorial page to Trumpian ideals, I would have laughed and said it wouldn’t – it couldn’t – happen. 

If there’s one thing I’ve learned over the past year, it’s not to take anything for granted.

The media sector in our small country is economically stressed: It’s battling international tech giants and AI models gobbling up digital revenue, and we’re all dealing with news fatigue and its cousin, hope fatigue.

The challenges are real, and becoming existential. Just look how many journalist jobs have been lost in the past decade (and it’s worsened in the past few years, with further job cuts and the closure of Newshub).

But there are still lots of journalists in New Zealand doing their very best in this tough environment, holding power to account on behalf of all of us. Because there’s another lesson for Aotearoa from the US: When the media is eroded or disappeared, our democracy clearly suffers. 

In the US, media analysts have noted the appearance of “news deserts” – places where there is virtually no credible local journalism. “Democracy suffers as citizens become less engaged and more polarised, and as government corruption flourishes because the watchdog has gone silent,” Margaret Sullivan, a former media columnist at the Washington Post and public editor at the New York Times, has written.

One study with a particularly jarring title, echoing the Post’s tagline – “Financing Dies in Darkness?” – found that when a newspaper closed, the city council had more trouble borrowing money. The markets concluded that local newspapers held their local governments accountable and kept costs low.

Other studies have shown that “news deserts” – in the US, as well as in the UK, Australia, Norway and Switzerland – have increased political polarisation, and reduced civic knowledge and voter turnout.

Despite everything that’s happened in the past few years, it is still clearly true that democracy does die in darkness. Here’s to sunlight.

Anna Fifield now writes about New Zealand’s place in the world on Substack and compiles the Spinoff’s weekly World Bulletin newsletter.
